y-m-21-01.title: If the angles measure the same, are the two lines parallel?
y-m-21-01.goal: Tell apart how differently a directly measured angle value and a condition given in the problem support a judgment about parallelism, and correct your judgment or confidence as new information comes in.
y-m-21-01.material: A line n meets two lines l and m. At two different points P and Q on n, the line n meets l and m respectively, and the distance between P and Q is 6cm (P is above, Q is below). Let ∠a (angle a) be the angle at P that is to the upper right of n, and ∠b (angle b) be the angle at Q in the same position, to the upper right of n. These two angles are corresponding angles. Jiho wants to know whether the lines l and m are parallel. Being parallel means that they never meet no matter how far you extend them. (There is no figure, so draw one in your head or on paper as described above.)
y-m-21-01.thinking.0: Judge the limits of measurement evidence
y-m-21-01.thinking.1: Correct your judgment and confidence with new information
y-m-21-01.thinking.2: Tell apart measured values from given conditions
y-m-21-01.prereq.0: The meaning of corresponding angles and how to find corresponding angles in a figure
y-m-21-01.prereq.1: The experience of learning the property 'if corresponding angles are equal, the two lines are parallel'
y-m-21-01.prereq.2: The experience of measuring angles with a protractor
y-m-21-01.s.s1.prompt: More information is given one piece at a time. At each step, choose the judgment you think fits what you know now. Then, looking at the later information, think about whether your judgment or confidence should change.
y-m-21-01.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, write separately the 'values obtained by measuring directly' and the 'conditions given in words in the problem'.
y-m-21-01.s.s1.hint.1: In your own words, estimate roughly how far away the place where the two lines meet would be if the value you read is off by 1°.
y-m-21-01.s.s1.st.0.info: Jiho measured with a protractor and read ∠a=65° and ∠b=65°. This protractor has marks every 1°, and a reading can be off by about 1°.
y-m-21-01.s.s1.st.0.ask: With the information now, can we say that lines l and m are parallel?
y-m-21-01.s.s1.st.0.after: The readings being equal is evidence for being parallel. But within a 1° error, it is hard to insist that they are exactly equal. So both 'it is likely' and 'it can't be decided yet' are fitting judgments right now.
y-m-21-01.s.s1.st.0.o.a: The readings are equal, so we can say for certain that they are parallel
y-m-21-01.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You took the readings being equal to mean that the two angles are exactly equal. Think also about the error that comes with reading.
y-m-21-01.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It is likely parallel. The same value came out, so for now I see it as parallel
y-m-21-01.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This is a judgment that took the same value coming out as a reason to see the likelihood as high.
y-m-21-01.s.s1.st.0.o.c: They are not parallel. Perfectly identical angles can't be made with a protractor
y-m-21-01.s.s1.st.0.r.c: 'It is hard to read exactly the same value' and 'the two angles are different' are different statements. The readings being equal is still evidence.
y-m-21-01.s.s1.st.0.o.d: It can't be decided yet. Even if they are off by about 1°, they can be read like this
y-m-21-01.s.s1.st.0.r.d: This judgment lowered the confidence by considering that there is a reading error.
y-m-21-01.s.s1.st.1.info: Jiho measured again with a more precise protractor and got ∠a=65° and ∠b=66°. If the two angles are exactly 65° and 66°, the two lines are not parallel, and when the distance between points P and Q is 6cm, a computer calculation shows they meet at a place about 2.8m away from line n. Jiho's paper is 30cm on a side.
y-m-21-01.s.s1.st.1.ask: Seeing this new information, how should your judgment or confidence change?
y-m-21-01.s.s1.st.1.after: Even with a 1° difference, the place where they meet is very far outside the paper, so they look parallel on the paper. Your confidence may change toward it being hard to decide from measured values alone whether they are parallel or not. Even so, if you kept your first judgment, it should be kept carefully as 'it could be parallel'.
y-m-21-01.s.s1.st.1.o.a: Conclude that they are not parallel, because the two values differ by 1°
y-m-21-01.s.s1.st.1.r.a: A 1° difference is within the reading error. It is too early to conclude from this difference alone that they are not parallel.
y-m-21-01.s.s1.st.1.o.b: I still think they could be parallel. 66° is also a value within the reading error
y-m-21-01.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You kept your judgment by considering the error. But what about the degree of confidence?
y-m-21-01.s.s1.st.1.o.c: The place where they meet is far outside the paper, so it is hard to decide from measured values alone
y-m-21-01.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You reflected in your confidence that the meeting place is so far away that it can't even be seen.
y-m-21-01.s.s1.st.1.o.d: Measuring with a protractor is useless, so it is better to decide by looking with your eyes
y-m-21-01.s.s1.st.1.r.d: With your eyes, it is even harder to tell a 1° difference than with a protractor. Knowing the limits of measuring is different from throwing measuring away.
y-m-21-01.s.s1.st.2.info: The teacher told you the condition of the problem. The problem says in words, '∠a and ∠b are equal.' and does not give values. This is not a measured value but a condition given in the problem.
y-m-21-01.s.s1.st.2.ask: From this condition alone, can we conclude that l and m are parallel?
y-m-21-01.s.s1.st.2.after: When 'the corresponding angles are equal' is given as a condition, you can say for certain that they are parallel even without knowing the sizes of the angles. Values obtained by measuring have error, but a given condition has no error.
y-m-21-01.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Yes. It is given that the corresponding angles are equal, so we can say they are parallel regardless of error
y-m-21-01.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You separated the fact that the 'equal' given as a condition is a settled fact, not a measured value.
y-m-21-01.s.s1.st.2.o.b: No. Without knowing how many degrees the angles are, we can't decide whether they are parallel
y-m-21-01.s.s1.st.2.r.b: Even though the fact that they are 'equal' is enough, you thought you could judge only if you knew the size of the angles.
y-m-21-01.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Yes, but Jiho must measure again with a protractor and check that the same value comes out
y-m-21-01.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You trust the directly measured value more than the given condition. If the measured value disagrees, you could also think the figure is not accurate.
y-m-21-01.s.s1.st.2.o.d: No. Jiho must measure again with a protractor and the two values must come out equal
y-m-21-01.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You thought it only becomes certain by measuring. Think about the difference between a condition given in words and a measured value.
y-m-21-01.s.s1.reflect: Compare your first judgment and your last judgment. Did the new information change the 'judgment itself' or 'how confident you are'? Think about how measured values and conditions given in the problem differ in how certain they are.
y-m-21-01.s.s2.prompt: Write it as if you were telling Jiho. (1) What your first judgment was and what it became at the end (if it did not change, why it stayed the same), (2) what basis there must be to say for certain that l and m are parallel.
y-m-21-01.s.s2.hint.0: Write the judgment you chose at first and the judgment you chose at the end side by side, and compare what is the same and what is different.
y-m-21-01.s.s2.hint.1: Write one sentence each for 'I found out by measuring' and 'it was given as a condition', and compare which is more certain.
y-m-21-01.s.s2.placeholder: Example: At first I thought ..., but ...
y-m-21-01.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you write by comparing what your first judgment was and how it ended up?
y-m-21-01.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you use the fact that measured values have error as a reason for your judgment?
y-m-21-01.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you separate the 'given condition' from the 'measured value' and say which one is certain?
y-m-21-01.s.s2.model.0: At first it measured 65° and 65°, so I thought it was likely parallel. But there is a 1° error, and even with 65° and 66° you can't tell them apart on paper, so I changed to thinking it can't be decided from measured values alone. If the problem gives that the corresponding angles are equal, I can say for certain that they are parallel without error.
y-m-21-01.s.s2.model.1: I thought from the start that it can't be decided yet, and it stays the same to the end. Because the protractor marks are every 1°, you can't tell apart a slight difference. To say it for certain, it must be given as a condition that the corresponding angles are equal.
y-m-21-01.s.s2.modelNote.1: The judgment stayed the same, but I wrote the reasons in light of the new information.

y-m-21-02.title: Two ways to find the sum of the interior angles, but the answers differ?
y-m-21-02.topic: Interior and exterior angles of polygons
y-m-21-02.goal: When the sums of interior angles found by two different methods differ, decide at which step it went wrong, and use the result to find regular polygons whose one interior angle is a natural number.
y-m-21-02.material: Two people found the sum of the interior angles of a convex pentagon (a pentagon in which all interior angles are less than 180°) using different methods. Harin: Draw all the diagonals from one vertex to the other vertices, dividing the pentagon into 3 triangles, and said 180°×3=540°. Doyun: Marked one point inside the pentagon and connected it to all five vertices, getting 5 triangles, and said 180°×5=900°. It is the same pentagon, but the answers differ. (The sum of the three interior angles of a triangle is 180°.)
y-m-21-02.thinking.0: Compare and evaluate the results of two methods
y-m-21-02.thinking.1: Find the cause of the disagreement
y-m-21-02.thinking.2: Make several examples that fit the conditions
y-m-21-02.prereq.0: The fact that the sum of the three interior angles of a triangle is 180°
y-m-21-02.prereq.1: The meanings of regular polygon, convex polygon, and diagonal
y-m-21-02.prereq.2: Checking whether a division comes out evenly
y-m-21-02.s.s1.prompt: Which explanation comparing the two people's methods is the most fitting?
y-m-21-02.s.s1.hint.0: Find whether any vertex of the triangles the two people drew is not a vertex of the pentagon.
y-m-21-02.s.s1.hint.1: Think about whether the angles gathered around that point are included in the interior angles of the pentagon.
y-m-21-02.s.s1.o.a: Doyun's 900° has the 360° of angles around the inside point mixed in, and if you subtract it, it becomes the same as Harin's 540°
y-m-21-02.s.s1.r.a: You checked whether all the angles of the divided triangles are interior angles of the pentagon, and you separated the angles around the inside point.
y-m-21-02.s.s1.o.b: Doyun's method, which gives 5 triangles, is more careful, so 900° is right and Harin left out the angles of 2 triangles
y-m-21-02.s.s1.r.b: You thought that more triangles means more accurate. Check whether all the angles of the triangles are interior angles of the pentagon.
y-m-21-02.s.s1.o.c: The shapes and numbers of the triangles the two people made are different, so both 540° and 900° can be the sum of the interior angles of the pentagon
y-m-21-02.s.s1.r.c: You thought the sum of interior angles of the same figure can differ depending on the method. Remember that it is the same pentagon.
y-m-21-02.s.s1.o.d: Harin's diagonals go out of only one vertex, so some of the pentagon's interior angles are left out of the triangles, and 540° is wrong
y-m-21-02.s.s1.r.d: You did not check whether the three triangles divided by the diagonals fill the pentagon without gaps.
y-m-21-02.s.s1.explain: If you add up all the angles of Doyun's 5 triangles, they include not only the interior angles of the pentagon but also the angles gathered around the inside point (sum 360°). 900°−360°=540°, so the answers of the two methods are the same. If you use the same methods on an n-gon, Harin gets (n−2) triangles, and Doyun subtracts 360° from n triangles.
y-m-21-02.s.s2.prompt: All the interior angles of a regular n-gon are equal. Find 3 different regular n-gons, with n from 10 to 40, whose one interior angle is a natural number (in degrees), and write n and the size x (°) of one interior angle.
y-m-21-02.s.s2.hint.0: First do the process of finding the sum of interior angles for a small case (such as a regular pentagon) and dividing by n to get one interior angle.
y-m-21-02.s.s2.hint.1: Choose an n and see whether one interior angle comes out to a natural number, and if not, change n.
y-m-21-02.s.s2.var.x: Size of one interior angle x (°)
y-m-21-02.s.s2.ok.c1: n is a natural number from 10 to 40.
y-m-21-02.s.s2.fail.c1: n must be a natural number from 10 to 40.
y-m-21-02.s.s2.ok.c2: The size of one interior angle is a natural number.
y-m-21-02.s.s2.fail.c2: The size of one interior angle x must be a natural number (in degrees).
y-m-21-02.s.s2.ok.c3: Adding one interior angle n times equals the sum of the interior angles of the n-gon.
y-m-21-02.s.s2.fail.c3: x added n times is not equal to the sum of the interior angles of the n-gon. Find the sum of the interior angles of the regular n-gon again.
y-m-21-02.s.s2.explain: The sum of the interior angles of an n-gon is 180°×(n−2), and one interior angle of a regular n-gon is that divided by n. The n for which this value is a natural number are 10, 12, 15, 18, 20, 24, 30, 36, 40. For example: n=10 is 1440°÷10=144°, n=12 is 1800°÷12=150°, n=15 is 2340°÷15=156°.
y-m-21-02.s.s3.prompt: n=14 is a number from 10 to 40, yet it is not in the list found above. Explain why one interior angle of a regular 14-gon is not a natural number (in degrees).
y-m-21-02.s.s3.hint.0: First find the sum of the interior angles of a regular 14-gon and divide it by 14.
y-m-21-02.s.s3.hint.1: Put the n that divide evenly and n=14 that does not divide evenly side by side and compare what is different.
y-m-21-02.s.s3.placeholder: Example: The sum of the interior angles of a regular 14-gon is ...
y-m-21-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write the sum of the interior angles (or one exterior angle) of the regular 14-gon as a number?
y-m-21-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you go on to write that dividing that number by 14 does not give a natural number?
y-m-21-02.s.s3.model.0: The sum of the interior angles of a regular 14-gon is 180°×12=2160°, and dividing this by 14 gives 154.28…°, so it doesn't divide evenly. So one interior angle is not a natural number.
y-m-21-02.s.s3.model.1: One exterior angle is 360°÷14, but 360 is not divisible by 14, so it is not a natural number. One interior angle is 180° minus one exterior angle, so likewise it is not a natural number.
y-m-21-02.s.s3.model.2: For an interior angle to be a natural number, n must be a divisor of 360, and 14 is not a divisor of 360.
y-m-21-02.s.s3.model.3: 2160÷14 doesn't divide evenly, so it isn't a natural number.

y-m-21-03.title: If the central angle is 3 times as large, is the chord also 3 times as long?
y-m-21-03.topic: Central angles, arcs, and chords of a sector
y-m-21-03.goal: Find the wrong line in a solution that applied the property that arc length is directly proportional to the central angle to chords as well, and confirm that chord length is not directly proportional using the cases of central angles 180° and 120°.
y-m-21-03.material: There is a circle O with a radius of 6cm. For points A, B, C on the circle, ∠AOB=60° and ∠AOC=180°. A chord is a line segment connecting two points on a circle. Seoyun solved as below to find the length of chord AC. Already known: In a sector, the arc length is directly proportional to the size of the central angle. (Triangle OAB is an equilateral triangle with all three sides 6cm, so chord AB=6cm.)
y-m-21-03.thinking.0: Find the error in a solution
y-m-21-03.thinking.1: Judge the range where a property applies
y-m-21-03.thinking.2: Test a generalization with a counterexample
y-m-21-03.prereq.0: The meanings of center, radius, chord, arc, and central angle of a circle
y-m-21-03.prereq.1: The property that arc length is directly proportional to the size of the central angle
y-m-21-03.prereq.2: The fact that the three sides of an equilateral triangle are equal in length
y-m-21-03.s.s1.prompt: This is the process by which Seoyun found the length of chord AC. Choose the one wrong line.
y-m-21-03.s.s1.hint.0: For each line, look at whether it follows directly from the line before or whether a new property has been brought in.
y-m-21-03.s.s1.hint.1: Recall whether the property 'is directly proportional' was learned for arcs or for chords.
y-m-21-03.s.s1.line.0: Triangle OAB has OA=OB=6cm and ∠AOB=60°, so it is an equilateral triangle, and chord AB=6cm.
y-m-21-03.s.s1.line.2: The size of the central angle and the arc length are directly proportional, so the chord length is also directly proportional to the size of the central angle.
y-m-21-03.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is wrong. The arc length is directly proportional to the size of the central angle, but the chord length is not. The 18cm in line 4 is a value that came from the wrong line 3 (if you chose line 4, you found that the result is wrong, but the cause is line 3).
y-m-21-03.s.s2.prompt: What is the most direct way to confirm that Seoyun's result of 18cm is wrong? (Think about chord AC with ∠AOC=180°.)
y-m-21-03.s.s2.hint.0: Draw how the three points A, O, C are placed when ∠AOC=180°.
y-m-21-03.s.s2.hint.1: Then express the length of AC directly using the radius and compare it with Seoyun's value.
y-m-21-03.s.s2.o.a: The circumference of the circle is 12π cm (about 37.7cm), so 18cm is shorter than the circumference and is a possible value
y-m-21-03.s.s2.r.a: You compared the chord length with the circumference of the circle. Think about whether that is a proper length to compare a chord with.
y-m-21-03.s.s2.o.b: It was 6cm at 60°, so at 180° 6×3=18cm is right, and I'll check the calculation once more
y-m-21-03.s.s2.r.b: You only rechecked the calculation with the same idea of proportion. Test the idea of proportion itself.
y-m-21-03.s.s2.o.c: If ∠AOC=180°, AC is a diameter passing through the center of the circle and is 12cm, so 18cm is longer than that and impossible
y-m-21-03.s.s2.r.c: You tested the result by focusing on the special shape of the central angle 180°.
y-m-21-03.s.s2.o.d: A chord is shorter than its arc, so comparing with the length of arc AC, 6π (about 18.8cm), 18cm is a possible value and Seoyun is right
y-m-21-03.s.s2.r.d: It is true that a chord is shorter than its arc. But this comparison alone does not tell you that 18cm is wrong.
y-m-21-03.s.s2.explain: If the central angle is 180°, chord AC is a diameter passing through the center O of the circle, so its length is 6+6=12cm. 18cm is longer than that and cannot be. The method of comparing with the arc (d) uses a true property but does not show that 18cm is wrong.
y-m-21-03.s.s3.prompt: Think about chord AD with central angle 120° (∠AOD=120°). If 'the chord length is also directly proportional', it should be 2 times that at 60°, 6×2=12cm. Is the actual AD longer than 12cm, the same, or shorter? Write why you think so.
y-m-21-03.s.s3.hint.0: Draw triangle AOD connecting the three points A, O, D and estimate the lengths of its three sides.
y-m-21-03.s.s3.hint.1: Put the chord lengths for central angles 60°, 120°, 180° side by side and compare how they change.
y-m-21-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you say in one way how AD compares with 12cm?
y-m-21-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you give visible evidence, such as triangle AOD or the values at 60° and 180°?
y-m-21-03.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you go on to the conclusion 'chord length is not directly proportional to the central angle'?
y-m-21-03.s.s3.model.0: AD is shorter than 12cm. In triangle AOD, OA+OD=6+6=12cm, and one side of a triangle must be shorter than the sum of the other two sides, so AD is shorter than 12cm. So the chord is not directly proportional to the central angle.
y-m-21-03.s.s3.model.1: I think it's shorter. At central angle 60° it's 6cm and at 180° it's 12cm, and 120° is between them, so it should be less than 12cm. When the central angle becomes 3 times as large (from 60° to 180°), the chord becomes only 2 times as long, so it's not a direct proportion.
y-m-21-03.s.s3.modelNote.1: This is an explanation that uses the fact that the chord gets longer as the central angle gets larger. You don't need to know the exact value.

y-m-21-04.title: Are two lines that don't meet parallel?
y-m-21-04.topic: Positional relationships of points, lines, and planes
y-m-21-04.goal: Using an example on a cube, confirm that in space two lines that don't meet may not be parallel, and say what more information is needed to conclude they are parallel.
y-m-21-04.material: There is a cube ABCD-EFGH. The top face is ABCD and the bottom face is EFGH, with E, F, G, H directly below A, B, C, D respectively. So AB, CD, EF, GH are four edges parallel to each other, AD, BC, EH, FG are also four edges parallel to each other, and AE, BF, CG, DH are also four edges parallel to each other. Think of a line as an edge extended endlessly in both directions. Seojin said, "If two lines don't meet, they are parallel."
y-m-21-04.thinking.2: Rewrite the conditions under which a claim holds
y-m-21-04.prereq.0: Positional relationships of two lines in a plane (they meet, they are parallel)
y-m-21-04.prereq.1: Names of the vertices and edges of a cube
y-m-21-04.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the lines that do not meet line AB and are also not parallel to AB. (Think of each as an edge extended endlessly in both directions.)
y-m-21-04.s.s1.hint.0: For each line among the options, first check whether it 'meets' AB, and if it doesn't, check whether it is 'parallel'.
y-m-21-04.s.s1.hint.1: Divide the edges of the cube into three groups by direction (length, width, height) and compare whether each is in the same group as AB.
y-m-21-04.s.s1.r.a: CD does not meet AB. Check whether the two lines are parallel (extend in the same direction).
y-m-21-04.s.s1.r.b: You checked the direction AB lies in, the direction CG extends in, and whether the two have a point where they meet.
y-m-21-04.s.s1.r.c: AD meets AB at point A. First check that it is a line that meets.
y-m-21-04.s.s1.r.d: You checked the direction AB lies in, the direction FG extends in, and whether the two have a point where they meet.
y-m-21-04.s.s1.r.e: EF is an edge parallel to AB. A parallel line does not count as a 'line that is not parallel'.
y-m-21-04.s.s1.explain: The lines that do not meet AB are CD, CG, FG, EF, and so on. Among these, CD and EF are parallel to AB, so they are parallel, while CG and FG neither meet AB nor are parallel to it. AD meets AB at point A.
y-m-21-04.s.s2.prompt: For Seojin's statement 'If two lines don't meet, they are parallel' to always be right, what more would have to be known about two lines that don't meet?
y-m-21-04.s.s2.hint.0: Put two lines drawn only on a plane and two lines drawn on a cube side by side and compare what is different.
y-m-21-04.s.s2.explain: Two lines on the same plane that don't meet are parallel. In space, there are two lines that are not on the same plane, so they neither meet nor are parallel.
y-m-21-04.s.s3.prompt: Rewrite Seojin's statement so that it is also true in space, and give an example of two lines (extended edges of the cube) that show why it needs to be fixed.
y-m-21-04.s.s3.hint.0: Among the two lines you chose as 'neither meeting nor parallel' in s1, choose one line to pair with AB.
y-m-21-04.s.s3.hint.1: Write the fixed statement and the counterexample as separate sentences first, and then connect them.
y-m-21-04.s.s3.placeholder: Example: Two lines on the same ... that ... For example, line ...
y-m-21-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you put a condition like 'lie on one plane' in the fixed statement?
y-m-21-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you check that the two lines you used as an example really neither meet nor are parallel?
y-m-21-04.s.s3.model.0: Two lines on the same plane that don't meet are parallel. In space, there are lines like line AB and line CG that neither meet nor are parallel, so a condition is needed.
y-m-21-04.s.s3.model.1: The two lines must be on one plane. For example, line AB and line FG don't meet but aren't parallel either, so you can't say they are parallel just because they don't meet.
y-m-21-04.s.s3.modelNote.1: You don't need to know the term 'skew lines'.
y-m-21-04.s.s2.hint.1: Try drawing one line you chose in s1 and AB together on one flat surface.
y-m-21-04.s.s2.o.a: The lengths of the edges of the two lines before extending are equal
y-m-21-04.s.s2.r.a: Length has nothing to do with being parallel. AB and CG have the same length but are not parallel.
y-m-21-04.s.s2.o.b: There is no place where the two lines meet at a right angle
y-m-21-04.s.s2.r.b: Whether they are perpendicular or not has nothing to do with being parallel. AB and CG, which extend in perpendicular directions, don't meet either.
y-m-21-04.s.s2.o.c: Both lines lie on one plane
y-m-21-04.s.s2.r.c: You focused on the condition of thinking of the two lines as lying on one plane.
y-m-21-04.s.s2.o.d: The two lines lie on different planes
y-m-21-04.s.s2.r.d: The condition that there is no plane they both lie on actually creates cases like AB and CG that neither meet nor are parallel. To be parallel, they must run side by side on one plane.

y-m-21-05.title: Let's sort out which shapes can become regular polyhedra
y-m-21-05.goal: Using the condition that the sum of the angles around a vertex must be less than 360°, find all the possible (face shape, number of faces meeting) without missing any, and tell apart whether that condition is a necessary condition or a sufficient condition.
y-m-21-05.material: A regular polyhedron is a convex solid whose faces are all congruent regular polygons and where the same number of faces meet at every vertex. Jiyun wants to find out whether she can make a regular polyhedron by gathering q faces that are regular polygons with p sides at each vertex. Call the sum of one interior angle of each of the regular p-gons gathered at one vertex the 'sum of the angles around the vertex'. For the vertex to be pointed as a solid, this sum must be less than 360° (if it is 360° it becomes flat, and if it is more than 360° it cannot fold). At least 3 faces meet at one vertex. One interior angle of a regular p-gon is 180°×(p−2)÷p.
y-m-21-05.thinking.0: Find all the possible cases within constraints without missing any
y-m-21-05.thinking.1: Tell apart necessary and sufficient conditions
y-m-21-05.thinking.2: Explain the reasons for impossible cases
y-m-21-05.prereq.0: The size of one interior angle of a regular polygon (regular triangle 60°, square 90°, regular pentagon 108°, regular hexagon 120°)
y-m-21-05.prereq.1: The meanings of polyhedron, face, and vertex
y-m-21-05.prereq.2: Making a table and examining the cases without missing any
y-m-21-05.s.s1.prompt: Find 3 different (p, q) for which the sum of the angles around the vertex is less than 360°. (p is the number of sides of one face, from 3 to 8. q is the number of faces meeting at one vertex, from 3 to 10.)
y-m-21-05.s.s1.hint.0: Choose a p, find one interior angle, and increase q from 3, checking until just before the sum reaches 360°.
y-m-21-05.s.s1.hint.1: Compare whether increasing q more is pointless once the sum becomes 360° or more.
y-m-21-05.s.s1.var.p: Number of sides of a face p
y-m-21-05.s.s1.var.q: Number of faces meeting at one vertex q
y-m-21-05.s.s1.ok.c1: p is a natural number from 3 to 8.
y-m-21-05.s.s1.fail.c1: p must be a natural number from 3 to 8.
y-m-21-05.s.s1.ok.c2: q is a natural number from 3 to 10.
y-m-21-05.s.s1.fail.c2: q must be a natural number from 3 to 10.
y-m-21-05.s.s1.ok.c3: The sum of the angles around the vertex is less than 360°.
y-m-21-05.s.s1.fail.c3: The sum of the angles around the vertex is not less than 360°. Multiply one interior angle by q to check.
y-m-21-05.s.s1.explain: One interior angle of a regular triangle (p=3) is 60°, so for q=3, 4, 5 the sums are 180°, 240°, 300°. A square (p=4) has 90°, so q=3 gives 270°, and a regular pentagon (p=5) has 108°, so q=3 gives 324°. These 5 are all there are. For q=6 (regular triangle) or q=4 (square), the sum is exactly 360°, and if p is 6 or more, q=3 alone already gives 360° or more.
y-m-21-05.s.s2.prompt: When p is from 3 to 8 and q is 3 or more, how many (p, q) are there in total with a sum less than 360°? (For each p, find out how far q can be increased.)
y-m-21-05.s.s2.hint.0: Make a table with one row each for p=3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, and first find the sum when q=3 for each.
y-m-21-05.s.s2.hint.1: Decide whether you need to look further at a p if the sum is already 360° or more when q=3.
y-m-21-05.s.s2.r.a: You may have missed some by not checking the whole range of possible q for each p. Check again how far q can go when p=3.
y-m-21-05.s.s2.r.b: You may have counted even the cases where the sum is exactly 360° (it becomes flat). Read again whether the condition is 'less than 360°'.
y-m-21-05.s.s2.r.c: You may have counted even the cases where p is 6 or more. Start by calculating how big one interior angle of a regular hexagon is.
y-m-21-05.s.s2.r.d: This is the result of checking the limit of q for each p and counting without missing any.
y-m-21-05.s.s2.explain: With p=3, q=3, 4, 5 (3 ways), with p=4, q=3, and with p=5, q=3, making 5 ways in all. If p is 6 or more, one interior angle is 120° or more, so q=3 alone already makes the sum 360° or more.
y-m-21-05.s.s3.hint.0: Write as sentences, separately, 'if it doesn't pass this condition, it can't be one' and 'if it passes this condition, it can be one'.
y-m-21-05.s.s3.hint.1: For the cases that passed the condition, think about what more you would have to do to confirm that statement.
y-m-21-05.s.s3.o.a: It has already been proved that there are exactly 5 regular polyhedra
y-m-21-05.s.s3.r.a: The condition that the sum is less than 360° is the minimum condition for becoming a solid. Whether the cases that pass the condition can actually be made has to be checked separately.
y-m-21-05.s.s3.o.b: There can't be more than 5 regular polyhedra. Which of them can actually be made has to be checked separately
y-m-21-05.s.s3.r.b: You separated the necessary condition from the sufficient condition.
y-m-21-05.s.s3.o.c: It has been proved that only some of the 5 are possible
y-m-21-05.s.s3.r.c: This condition gives no reason that some of the cases that passed are impossible. Think about what reason you used to say only some are possible.
y-m-21-05.s.s3.o.d: Cases that did not pass the condition could also become regular polyhedra if folded, so there could be more than 5
y-m-21-05.s.s3.r.d: You missed the earlier condition that if the sum is 360° or more, it becomes flat or crumpled.
y-m-21-05.s.s3.explain: If the sum of the angles is not less than 360°, it can't become a regular polyhedron, so there are no more than 5. But passing does not guarantee that it can actually be made, so you need to build a model or check by another method (in fact all 5 can be made: regular tetrahedron, regular octahedron, regular icosahedron, cube, regular dodecahedron).
y-m-21-05.s.s4.prompt: (p, q)=(6, 3), that is, gathering 3 regular hexagon faces at one vertex, was left out by the condition. Show the reason by calculation, and say what actually happens if you gather them like this.
y-m-21-05.s.s4.hint.0: Find the size of one interior angle of a regular hexagon and add 3 of them.
y-m-21-05.s.s4.hint.1: Compare the sum with 360° and imagine what happens around the vertex.
y-m-21-05.s.s4.placeholder: Example: One interior angle of a regular hexagon is ... If you gather 3 ...
y-m-21-05.s.s4.selfAssess.0: Did you calculate one interior angle of a regular hexagon, 120°, and the sum of 3 of them?
y-m-21-05.s.s4.selfAssess.1: Did you go on to say that if the sum is 360°, the vertex does not become pointed and becomes flat?
y-m-21-05.s.s4.model.0: One interior angle of a regular hexagon is 120°, and gathering 3 gives a sum of 360°. Then the vertex doesn't become pointed but becomes a flat surface (a honeycomb shape), so it doesn't become a solid.
y-m-21-05.s.s4.model.1: The sum of the angles at a vertex must be less than 360° for it to fold, but 120°×3=360°, so it is exactly flat. So it doesn't fold and a solid isn't made.
y-m-21-05.s.s3.prompt: Suppose you found all the (p, q) that satisfy the conditions above. What can you say about regular polyhedra from this result alone?

y-m-21-06.title: Cans with the same volume: which design uses the least sheet metal?
y-m-21-06.topic: Volume and surface area of prisms and cylinders
y-m-21-06.material: You want to make a cylinder-shaped canned food can. The volume of the can is fixed at 36π cm³ (the volume of a cylinder is π×(radius of the base)×(radius of the base)×(height)). The top and bottom lids and the side are all sheet metal, and the surface area is 2π×r×r+2π×r×h (r is the radius of the base, h is the height, in cm). Ignore the thickness of the sheet metal and the seams. The less sheet metal is used, the lower the cost, but it is also important whether people find it convenient to use. The radius and height are both chosen as natural numbers.
y-m-21-06.prereq.0: How to find the volume and surface area of a cylinder (the formulas are in the material)
y-m-21-06.s.s1.prompt: Make at least 3 different designs (r, h) of a cylinder-shaped can with a volume of 36π cm³. The base radius r (cm) and height h (cm) are natural numbers.
y-m-21-06.s.s1.hint.0: In the volume formula π×r×r×h, drop the π and find the cases where r×r×h is 36.
y-m-21-06.s.s1.hint.1: Choose r starting from 1 and check whether h comes out as a natural number.
y-m-21-06.s.s1.ok.c1: r and h are natural numbers.
y-m-21-06.s.s1.fail.c1: r and h must be natural numbers 1 or more.
y-m-21-06.s.s1.fail.c2: The volume (π×r×r×h) is not 36π. Check whether r×r×h is 36.
y-m-21-06.s.s1.explain: The natural numbers that satisfy r×r×h=36 are only four: (r, h)=(1, 36), (2, 9), (3, 4), (6, 1). h is a natural number only when r×r is a divisor of 36.
y-m-21-06.s.s2.prompt: Find the surface area of each of the four designs (surface area=2π×r×r+2π×r×h). How does the surface area change as r grows through 1, 2, 3, 6?
y-m-21-06.s.s2.hint.0: For each of the four designs, calculate 2×r×r and 2×r×h separately and write them in a table.
y-m-21-06.s.s2.hint.1: In the table, compare how each of the two terms moves as r gets bigger and what happens to the sum.
y-m-21-06.s.s2.o.a: The bigger r gets, the surface area keeps only decreasing
y-m-21-06.s.s2.r.a: When r gets bigger, the side gets smaller but the lids get bigger. Think about whether you calculated the surface area for r=6, h=1 too.
y-m-21-06.s.s2.explain: Dropping π and calculating 2r²+2rh, (1, 36) is 74, (2, 9) is 44, (3, 4) is 42, and (6, 1) is 84. It decreases from 74 to 44 to 42, then increases again to 84.
y-m-21-06.s.s3.prompt: Choose one design that uses the least sheet metal, and explain the reason with the surface area values. Then add one thing besides surface area that should be considered when designing an actual can.
y-m-21-06.s.s3.hint.0: Write the surface area of the design you chose and the surface areas of the other designs side by side as numbers.
y-m-21-06.s.s3.hint.1: Think of real uses, such as gripping, stacking, and what it will hold.
y-m-21-06.s.s3.placeholder: Example: I'll choose r=..., h=.... The surface area is ...
y-m-21-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you compare the surface area of the chosen design with the other designs using numbers?
y-m-21-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you think about other points instead of saying that the design with the smallest surface area is always the best?
y-m-21-06.s.s3.model.0: r=3, h=4 has a surface area of 42π, the smallest of the four, so it uses the least sheet metal. But its diameter is 6cm, so it may be uncomfortable to hold in one hand, so use should be considered too.
y-m-21-06.goal: Make several designs yourself and compare them to show that the surface area can differ even when the volume is the same, choose the design that uses the least material by the surface area value, and also state one other thing to consider besides surface area.
y-m-21-06.s.s2.o.b: As r gets bigger, the surface area only keeps increasing
y-m-21-06.s.s2.r.b: r=1, h=36 is a very thin, long can. Think about whether you calculated the surface area of this can.
y-m-21-06.s.s2.o.c: The volumes are the same, so the surface areas of the four designs are also all the same
y-m-21-06.s.s2.r.c: Having the same volume and having the same surface area are different things. Calculate and compare the surface areas of the two designs yourself.
y-m-21-06.s.s2.o.d: It decreases, then increases again after r=3
y-m-21-06.s.s2.r.d: You checked in the table that the areas of the side and the lid move in opposite directions.
y-m-21-06.s.s3.model.1: The design that uses the least sheet metal is r=3, h=4, with a surface area of 42π. It differs from r=2, h=9 (44π) by only 2π, so we should also consider whether it is easy to hold in one hand and good for stacking on a shelf.
y-m-21-06.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer that picks the design that uses the least and then adds another criterion.

y-m-21-07.title: Fixing an explanation of why the perpendicular bisector construction works
y-m-21-07.goal: Find and fix the wrong line in the justification of the perpendicular bisector construction, and explain by testing directly what condition the compass opening length must meet for the construction to work.
y-m-21-07.material: The length of segment AB is 10cm. Draw arcs with the same radius r (cm) centered at A and at B, above and below segment AB, to get the two points P and Q where they meet, and drawing line PQ gives the perpendicular bisector of AB. This compass opens to at most 12cm. Jiyun explained why PQ is the perpendicular bisector as below.
y-m-21-07.thinking.0: Find the wrong line in an argument
y-m-21-07.thinking.1: Find the condition under which the construction works
y-m-21-07.thinking.2: Explain what happens when the condition is broken
y-m-21-07.prereq.0: The steps for constructing the perpendicular bisector of a segment with an unmarked ruler and a compass
y-m-21-07.prereq.2: The experience of drawing arcs with a compass
y-m-21-07.s.s1.prompt: Jiyun drew arcs with the same radius r (cm) centered at the two endpoints A and B of segment AB (length 10cm) to get the upper and lower intersection points P and Q. She explained why line PQ is the perpendicular bisector of AB (a line that meets AB at a right angle and passes through the midpoint of AB) as follows. Choose the one wrong line.
y-m-21-07.s.s1.hint.1: For each line, look at whether it uses only what came from the line before and whether any newly inserted statement is right.
y-m-21-07.s.s1.line.0: The radii of the two arcs are the same, so AP=BP=AQ=BQ.
y-m-21-07.s.s1.line.1: All four sides are equal in length, so quadrilateral APBQ is a rhombus.
y-m-21-07.s.s1.line.2: All four angles of a rhombus are equal in size, so the diagonal PQ and AB meet at a right angle.
y-m-21-07.s.s1.line.3: The two diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other, so PQ passes through the midpoint of AB.
y-m-21-07.s.s1.line.4: So line PQ meets AB at a right angle and passes through the midpoint of AB.
y-m-21-07.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is wrong. A rhombus only has four equal sides, and its four angles are not all equal (if all four angles are equal, it is a square). The diagonals meeting at a right angle is a different property of a rhombus and needs its own reason. The conclusion is right but the reason in line 3 is wrong.
y-m-21-07.s.s2.prompt: When AB=10cm, find 3 different values of r for which you can open the compass to r cm and get the upper and lower intersection points P and Q by the same method. (r is a natural number, and this compass opens up to 12cm.)
y-m-21-07.s.s2.hint.0: Draw segment AB, mark the range reached by r from A and by r from B, and see whether the two arcs can meet.
y-m-21-07.s.s2.var.r: Length of the compass opening r (cm)
y-m-21-07.s.s2.ok.c1: r is a natural number from 1 to 12.
y-m-21-07.s.s2.fail.c1: r must be a natural number from 1 to 12.
y-m-21-07.s.s2.ok.c2: The two arcs meet each other.
y-m-21-07.s.s2.fail.c2: The two arcs do not meet, or meet at only one point, so you cannot get the two points P and Q.
y-m-21-07.s.s2.explain: If r is 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, the two arcs meet at two points. r must be greater than half of AB (5), and with this compass up to 12 is possible. If r=5, they touch at only one point, the midpoint of A and B, and if r<5, they don't meet.
y-m-21-07.s.s3.prompt: Explain what happens if you open the compass to r=5cm or r=4cm. Draw a picture and write in words why you can't draw the perpendicular bisector.
y-m-21-07.s.s3.hint.0: Draw AB, mark on AB the points reached by r from A and from B, and see how the two marks are placed.
y-m-21-07.s.s3.hint.1: Put r=5 and r=4 side by side and compare the gap or overlap between the two marks.
y-m-21-07.s.s3.placeholder: Example: If r=5, the two arcs ... If r=4 ...
y-m-21-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write separately what happens for r=5 and for r=4?
y-m-21-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you explain the reason by comparing with half of AB (5cm)?
y-m-21-07.s.s3.model.0: If r=5, the arc drawn from A and the arc drawn from B meet at only one place, the midpoint of AB, so there is only one intersection point. If r=4, the two arcs are about 2cm apart on AB and don't meet each other. In both cases you can't get two intersection points, upper and lower, so you can't draw the line.
y-m-21-07.s.s3.model.1: If you open the compass less than 5cm, which is half of AB, the two arcs don't touch each other. At exactly 5cm, they touch at one point, the midpoint, and one point alone cannot determine a line.
y-m-21-07.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer that explains r=5 and r<5 at once.
y-m-21-07.prereq.1: The meaning of a rhombus (a quadrilateral with four equal sides) and the property of a rhombus's diagonals (they bisect each other perpendicularly)
y-m-21-07.s.s1.hint.0: Write which property of a rhombus each line uses, and check whether that property is always true for a rhombus.
y-m-21-07.s.s2.hint.1: Change r from small to large values and find and compare when the two arcs first start to meet.
y-m-21-07.s.s3.model.2: If r=5, the two arcs touch only at the midpoint of AB, so there is only one point and you can't draw a line. If r=4, the two arcs are apart and can't touch each other, so there is no intersection point.

y-m-21-08.title: Is the cross-section of a solid of revolution always a circle?
y-m-21-08.topic: Solids of revolution and their cross-sections
y-m-21-08.goal: Show with a counterexample that the cross-section of a solid of revolution cut by a plane perpendicular to the axis of rotation is not always a circle, and explain the conditions under which the cross-section becomes a circle or a ring depending on the position of the figure.
y-m-21-08.material: A solid made by rotating a plane figure once around a line (the axis of rotation) is called a solid of revolution. Minjae said, "If you cut a solid of revolution with a plane perpendicular to the axis of rotation, the cross-section is always a circle." The figure being rotated lies on the same plane as the axis of rotation and is placed on only one side, without crossing the axis.
y-m-21-08.thinking.1: Make a counterexample and explain the conditions
y-m-21-08.prereq.0: The meanings of solid of revolution and axis of rotation
y-m-21-08.prereq.1: Which figures are rotated to make a cylinder, a cone, and a sphere
y-m-21-08.prereq.2: Finding the area of a circle (π×radius×radius)
y-m-21-08.s.s1.prompt: In which case can you make a counterexample to Minjae's statement 'If you cut a solid of revolution with a plane perpendicular to the axis of rotation, the cross-section is always a circle'? (Choose the solid of revolution whose cut cross-section is not a circle.)
y-m-21-08.s.s1.hint.0: Draw the case where the rotated figure touches the axis and the case where it is apart from the axis, and imagine the rotated shapes.
y-m-21-08.s.s1.hint.1: For each option, compare what happens after rotating to the part near the axis.
y-m-21-08.s.s1.o.a: Rotate a right triangle once so that one of the two sides forming the right angle lies on the axis
y-m-21-08.s.s1.r.a: A cone is made. The cross-section cut perpendicular to the axis is a circle. Draw the cross-section yourself to see whether it is a counterexample.
y-m-21-08.s.s1.o.b: Rotate a rectangle once so that one side lies on the axis of rotation
y-m-21-08.s.s1.r.b: A cylinder is made. The cross-section perpendicular to the axis is a circle everywhere.
y-m-21-08.s.s1.o.c: Rotate a rectangle once so that one side is parallel to the axis and 2cm away from it
y-m-21-08.s.s1.r.c: You thought about what happens in the middle when the figure is apart from the axis.
y-m-21-08.s.s1.o.d: Rotate a semicircle once so that its diameter lies on the axis of rotation
y-m-21-08.s.s1.r.d: A sphere is made. The cross-section cut perpendicular to the axis is a circle.
y-m-21-08.s.s1.explain: If a rectangle is apart from the axis, rotating it makes a pipe that is hollow in the middle. If you cut it perpendicular to the axis, the cross-section is a ring shape that is empty in the middle. In the other three cases, the figure touches the axis, so the cross-section is a full circle.
y-m-21-08.s.s2.prompt: If you place a rectangular metal sheet whose side parallel to the axis is 4cm from a cm away from the axis to b cm away and rotate it, you get a hollow pipe. Make 2 different (a, b) so that the area of the cross-section (ring) of this pipe cut perpendicular to the axis is 48π cm². (The area of the ring is π×b×b−π×a×a, a and b are natural numbers, and 1≤a<b≤13)
y-m-21-08.s.s2.hint.0: Choose a b, and find an a such that π×b×b minus 48π is π×a×a.
y-m-21-08.s.s2.hint.1: For b×b−a×a to be 48, b×b must be greater than 48, so narrow down the range of b.
y-m-21-08.s.s2.ok.c1: a and b are natural numbers that fit the conditions.
y-m-21-08.s.s2.fail.c1: a and b must be natural numbers with 1≤a<b≤13.
y-m-21-08.s.s2.ok.c2: The area of the ring is 48π.
y-m-21-08.s.s2.fail.c2: The area of the ring (π×b×b−π×a×a) is not 48π. Calculate b×b−a×a.
y-m-21-08.s.s2.explain: The (a, b) that satisfy b×b−a×a=48 are (1, 7), (4, 8), (11, 13). 49−1=48, 64−16=48, 169−121=48. If you change it to (b−a)×(b+a)=48 and look for cases where the product of two numbers is 48, you get the same result.
y-m-21-08.s.s3.prompt: Rewrite Minjae's statement into a true one, and explain how the cases where the cross-section is a circle and where it is a ring are separated depending on the position of the figure.
y-m-21-08.s.s3.hint.0: Think of the pipes in s1 and s2, and write what happens to the middle of the cross-section when the figure is apart from the axis.
y-m-21-08.s.s3.hint.1: Put it side by side with the cross-section when a figure touching the axis is rotated (a cylinder or a sphere) and compare.
y-m-21-08.s.s3.placeholder: Example: It is not always a circle. If the figure is ... from the axis, ...
y-m-21-08.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you say in one sentence how you changed 'always a circle'?
y-m-21-08.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you explain the case where the figure touches the axis and the case where it is apart from it separately?
y-m-21-08.s.s3.model.0: It is not always a circle. If the rotated figure touches the axis, the cross-section is a full circle, and if it is apart from the axis, the cross-section is a ring shape that is empty in the middle.
y-m-21-08.s.s3.model.1: It should be changed to 'a circle or a ring shape'. A hollow solid of revolution like a pipe is made by rotating a figure apart from the axis, so there is a hole in the cross-section, and a cylinder or a sphere is made with the figure touching the axis, so it is a circle.
y-m-21-08.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer that writes the two cases separately, for example.
